question: For projected SGD with a fixed learning rate on scale-invariant neural networks, can the observed weight trajectories be described as stationary distributions that minimize Helmholtz free energy, and does the effective temperature behave differently when every per-example gradient can vanish at an optimum?

key_findings.claim: Across the selected stationary learning-rate ranges, the authors recover a well-defined effective temperature that rises monotonically with learning rate in every tested underparameterized architecture-dataset pair.
key_findings.evidence: For projected ConvNet and ResNet-18 training on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, stationary loss and the k-nearest-neighbor trajectory-entropy estimate rise with learning rate. On the prespecified interior LR segments, the fitted temperature makes the observed LR an epsilon-minimizer of U-TS and is monotone. Very slow, nonstationary runs and high-LR random-walk runs are excluded before fitting.

key_findings.claim: The free-energy-minimization condition is satisfied by construction once temperature is chosen; the empirical content is the existence, stability, and monotonicity of that temperature, not an independently predicted minimum.
key_findings.evidence: For each target learning rate eta*, the method chooses T(eta*) so that F(eta*) is within epsilon of the lowest free energy among the sampled learning rates, equivalently using dU/dS after smoothing. The paper then treats broad definability and monotone growth of T with eta as the validation criteria.

key_findings.claim: Moderate-learning-rate overparameterized runs resemble the underparameterized stationary regime, whereas low-learning-rate overparameterized runs show a falling time-local temperature and continued convergence rather than a nonzero-loss stationary plateau.
key_findings.evidence: For the OP ConvNet on CIFAR-10, LRs from 10^-3 to 10^-2 yield stationary loss and entropy and an increasing fitted temperature. At smaller LRs, both quantities continue to decrease, so the stationary estimator is replaced by finite differences T_i=Delta U_i/Delta S_i; the curves fall toward zero. The same qualitative temperature decay appears for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and ConvNet on CIFAR-100, although the last case requires smoothing because raw ratios often become negative.

key_findings.claim: The analytic toy model supports a sharp UP-OP distinction in stochastic-gradient signal-to-noise behavior near a common optimum.
key_findings.evidence: A local quadratic lemma shows that, when all component gradients vanish, full and component gradients decay proportionally along any fixed approach direction and the limiting SNR is positive outside Hessian null directions. For the two-great-circle sphere model, Theorem 1 derives the SNR exactly, proves that the central meridian minimizes it, and proves convergence from below to a positive direction-dependent limit. The three-circle UP construction instead has zero SNR at its positive-loss optimum.

key_findings.claim: The neural-network SNR measurements only partially match the ideal overparameterized theory, and the mismatch shrinks as the dataset is reduced or the model is widened.
key_findings.evidence: In the baseline OP ConvNet trained on all 50,000 CIFAR-10 examples at LR 2e-5, mean stochastic-gradient norm scales against full-gradient norm with exponent about 0.78 rather than the theoretical value 1, and SNR keeps falling. Smaller CIFAR-10 subsets move the exponent toward 1. The wider OP ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 shows stabilized SNR while both gradient norms decline, which the authors interpret as stronger effective overparameterization.

key_findings.claim: The reported thermodynamic pattern is robust across two image datasets and two scale-invariant architectures, but it is not evaluated as a predictor of generalization or training efficiency.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 8-11 repeat the stationary-loss, entropy, fitted-temperature, free-energy, and low-LR temperature-decay plots for ConvNet and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The paper reports roughly 2,500 GPU-hours but no held-out-quality or wall-clock comparison tied to the free-energy quantities.

method.core_idea: Treat expected training loss as internal energy and differential entropy of the stationary weight distribution as thermodynamic entropy, then infer the effective temperature at each fixed learning rate from the slope of the empirical energy-entropy curve.
method.mechanism: The experiments constrain scale-invariant trainable weights to the unit sphere so the effective learning rate stays fixed. Projected SGD runs for up to 1.6 million iterations with independently sampled batches. A sliding window of 1,000 consecutive weights is converted to a k-nearest-neighbor graph, whose total edge length estimates entropy up to an additive constant. For stationary runs, temperature is selected so the target LR minimizes U-TS over the LR grid within an experiment-specific tolerance. For convergent low-LR OP runs, temperature is estimated along time by finite differences Delta U/Delta S. Gradient SNR, a two- or three-component spherical toy loss, a local quadratic lemma, and subset-size sweeps probe why the UP and OP regimes differ.
assumptions: A long finite trajectory at fixed LR is an adequate sample from a stationary or quasi-stationary weight distribution.
The high-dimensional k-nearest-neighbor graph statistic preserves the ordering and local slopes of true differential entropy even when its absolute value is biased.
Projecting all scale-invariant parameters to a unit sphere and freezing the classifier head preserves the SGD phenomena of interest while removing effective-LR drift.
The selected and smoothed U-versus-S curve is sufficiently regular that its slope defines a scalar temperature and a meaningful global free-energy comparison across LRs.
The operational OP condition is that every stochastic gradient vanishes at a shared optimum; parameter count alone is not the definition.
A local quadratic approximation describes the relative decay of full and per-example gradients close enough to an OP optimum.
Holding batch size at 128 makes learning rate the only intended control of update noise.

techniques.role: Projects scale-invariant parameters onto the unit sphere after every SGD update so nominal and effective learning rates do not separate through norm growth.
Uses total edge length in k-nearest-neighbor graphs over 1,000 consecutive weight vectors to estimate differential entropy up to a distribution-independent additive constant.
Finds the temperature interval for which each observed LR is an epsilon-minimizer of U-TS over the sampled stationary distributions.
Estimates a time-local temperature Delta U/Delta S when low-LR OP training has not reached a stationary ensemble.
Compares the full-gradient norm with root-mean-square stochastic-gradient deviations to distinguish persistent noise from jointly vanishing gradients.
Changes width and per-class dataset size to test whether stochastic and full gradients approach the equal decay rate predicted by the OP theory.
Constructs great-circle component losses with or without a common zero and permits exact visualization and proof of direction-dependent SNR limits.

evaluations.setting: UP ConvNet on CIFAR-10; projected SGD; batch 128; 1.6 million iterations; stationary LR segment [1.8e-4, 1.0e-2]
evaluations.metric: Existence and monotonicity of fitted T(eta), with free-energy epsilon-minimization
evaluations.result: T is well-defined over the retained segment and increases monotonically; U and S also rise with LR before their high-LR saturation regime.
evaluations.baseline: Excluded smallest LRs had not stabilized, while excluded largest LRs approached the uniform-sphere random-walk regime.

evaluations.setting: OP ConvNet on CIFAR-10; projected SGD; batch 128; width 64
evaluations.metric: Stationary fitted temperature at moderate LR and time-local Delta U/Delta S at low LR
evaluations.result: Moderate LRs from about 1e-3 to 1e-2 show stationary free-energy behavior; low LRs show temperature decaying toward zero while loss and entropy keep decreasing.
evaluations.baseline: The UP width-8 model retains positive stationary temperature instead of entering the low-LR convergence regime.

evaluations.setting: ConvNet and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, each in UP and OP widths
evaluations.metric: Cross-setting replication of monotone stationary T(eta) and low-LR OP temperature decay
evaluations.result: The same qualitative split appears in all four architecture-dataset pairs; the OP ConvNet/CIFAR-100 time-local estimate requires smoothing because unsmoothed values are noisy and often negative.
evaluations.baseline: The main-text ConvNet/CIFAR-10 experiment serves as the reference pattern for Appendix Figures 8-11.

evaluations.setting: Two-great-circle OP and three-great-circle UP loss functions on a unit 3D sphere; batch size 1; 50,000 steps or OP loss below 1e-16
evaluations.metric: Loss convergence, gradient norms, and asymptotic SNR across learning rates
evaluations.result: All displayed OP LRs converge to the common optimum with both gradient norms vanishing and positive limiting SNR; UP trajectories retain nonzero fluctuations whose radius grows with LR and whose limiting SNR tends toward zero as LR shrinks.
evaluations.baseline: The UP construction has no shared zero of its three component losses, unlike the OP construction.

evaluations.setting: OP ConvNet on CIFAR-10 subsets; LR 2e-5
evaluations.metric: Power-law exponent relating mean stochastic-gradient norm to full-gradient norm
evaluations.result: The full 50,000-example setup has exponent approximately 0.78; reducing dataset size moves the exponent toward the theoretical OP value 1.
evaluations.baseline: Lemma 1 predicts exponent exactly 1 under a local quadratic model when all component gradients vanish at the same optimum.

evaluations.metric: End-to-end reproducibility from the documented launch command
evaluations.result: Training, entropy, SNR, toy, and plotting code are present, but no result traces or pinned dependency versions are included. The provided launcher passes --seed and --loss while run.py accepts --seeds and --loss_fn, so the documented command does not run unchanged; requirements.txt also omits the imported torchvision dependency.
evaluations.baseline: A self-contained artifact would execute the README command and include exact environment and result inputs for the plotting notebooks.

limitations: Author-stated: batch size is fixed even though it also changes SGD noise and is central to conventional temperature definitions.
Author-stated: only plain SGD is studied; momentum, Adam, weight decay, and other practical optimizers are outside scope.
Author-stated: the nonparametric entropy estimate may be biased in the very high-dimensional weight spaces used here.

Reviewer-identified: temperature is fitted from the same U-S curve used to demonstrate free-energy minimization, so the minimum itself is not an out-of-sample prediction; monotonicity is the main non-tautological empirical test.

Reviewer-identified: learning-rate endpoints are excluded, curves are smoothed, and epsilon tolerances differ across experiments; no held-out LR grid or preregistered selection test quantifies sensitivity to those choices.

Reviewer-identified: 1,000 consecutive iterates are autocorrelated rather than independent samples, and the code uses Euclidean chord distances on the sphere; both choices can affect the entropy slope that defines temperature.

Reviewer-identified: the empirical domain is restricted to projected, fully scale-invariant ConvNet and ResNet-18 variants with frozen final layers on CIFAR-10/100, not ordinary unconstrained networks or foundation-model training.

Reviewer-identified: the OP neural-network experiments do not cleanly satisfy the theory's shared-zero-gradient premise; the main CIFAR-10 exponent is 0.78, and the authors state that resolving its asymptotic regime may exceed numerical precision.

Reviewer-identified: uncertainty bands are based on points within a run rather than independent training seeds, and the public launcher fixes seed 1; robustness to initialization and batch-stream randomness is therefore not established.

Reviewer-identified: no downstream generalization, scheduler, or optimizer-design benefit is tested, so the framework is descriptive within the measured regimes rather than validated as an actionable training rule.

Reviewer-identified: the code artifact lacks pinned package versions and saved result traces, requirements.txt omits the imported torchvision dependency, and its README launch path passes two incompatible flags (--seed versus --seeds and --loss versus --loss_fn).
failure_modes: If the empirical U-S frontier is nonconvex, loops back, or has nearly equal entropy at distinct losses, no unique positive scalar temperature will make every observed state a free-energy minimum.

Slow mixing or metastability can make one finite trajectory look stationary while sampling only one basin, causing the trajectory entropy to describe the run rather than an optimizer-wide equilibrium.
Noisy or sign-changing Delta S makes the time-local ratio Delta U/Delta S unstable or negative, as observed before smoothing in the OP ConvNet/CIFAR-100 experiment.
Weight-norm drift, partial scale invariance, trainable heads, weight decay, or adaptive preconditioning can change the effective LR and invalidate the fixed-volume unit-sphere analogy.
Strongly anisotropic gradient noise can sustain probability currents or limit cycles rather than an equilibrium Gibbs distribution, weakening a scalar Helmholtz-potential description.
A nominally wide model can remain insufficiently interpolating at the per-example-gradient level, yielding the sublinear gradient-decay exponent observed in the paper instead of the ideal OP regime.

Entropy-estimator bias that varies with LR, autocorrelation, curvature, or intrinsic dimension can create an apparently monotone temperature even when true differential entropy does not follow the same curve.
reusable_insights: A thermodynamic analogy becomes testable only after specifying which state variables are measured and what observation could make the inferred temperature undefined or nonmonotone.
For scale-invariant networks, controlling parameter norm is essential when studying learning-rate effects because norm growth otherwise silently anneals the effective LR.
Separating persistent per-example gradient noise from jointly vanishing gradients is more informative than labeling a model overparameterized solely by parameter count.
The decay exponent between stochastic- and full-gradient norms is a useful empirical diagnostic of how closely a training problem approaches the shared-zero-gradient interpolation regime.
Time-local ratios such as Delta U/Delta S can extend stationary-state analyses into convergent regimes, but smoothing and denominator stability must be audited explicitly.
An objective fitted to place every observation on its lower envelope should be evaluated through held-out predictions, monotonicity, or intervention—not by the fitted minimum alone.
open_questions: Does a temperature function fitted on some learning rates correctly predict the stationary distribution or loss-entropy trade-off at held-out learning rates?
How do temperature and free-energy curves change jointly with batch size, momentum, Adam preconditioning, and weight decay?
Can entropy be estimated with intrinsic-dimensional, geodesic, or spectral methods that remain reliable for autocorrelated high-dimensional trajectories?
Do unconstrained partially normalized networks exhibit the same UP-OP transition after effective learning rate is measured rather than fixed by projection?
Can the inferred thermodynamic variables predict a scheduler, generalization outcome, or transfer property better than LR and training loss alone?
What finite-time diagnostic distinguishes global stationarity from metastable residence in one basin?
Does the stochastic/full-gradient decay exponent converge to 1 in realistic interpolating networks before finite precision dominates?
Can anisotropic non-equilibrium currents be incorporated into a vector or matrix-valued generalization of the scalar-temperature framework?

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic gradient descent performs variational inference, converges to limit cycles for deep networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest prior free-energy and non-equilibrium account
competitive_landscape.difference: Chaudhari and Soatto derive variational optimization of an averaged potential plus entropy and emphasize anisotropic-noise limit cycles; this paper instead uses the original training loss as energy, empirically infers temperature from stationary LR sweeps, and does not model probability currents.

competitive_landscape.title: Energy-entropy competition and the effectiveness of stochastic gradient descent in machine learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. make undersampling, expressed through the parameter-to-data relation, the effective temperature and connect energy-entropy competition to wide minima and generalization. This paper holds architecture and data fixed, treats LR as the temperature control, and measures entropy along projected-SGD trajectories.

competitive_landscape.title: Noise and Fluctuation of Finite Learning Rate Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu, Ziyin, and Ueda derive exact discrete-time stationary covariances for quadratic losses, including momentum and adaptive second-order methods, and show that finite-LR fluctuations can depart sharply from SDE predictions. This paper sacrifices exact distributional theory for empirical entropy and temperature curves in nonlinear scale-invariant networks.

competitive_landscape.title: On the different regimes of Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Sclocchi and Wyart prescribe T=eta/B and derive a batch-size-learning-rate phase diagram separating noise-dominated SGD, a large-first-step regime, and gradient descent. This paper fixes B, infers T from U-S slopes, and separates regimes by whether per-example gradients can jointly vanish.

competitive_landscape.title: Parameter Symmetry and Noise Equilibrium of Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Ziyin et al. prove noise-driven motion along exponential symmetry directions toward noise equilibria and use balance conditions to explain sharpening, flattening, and representation formation. This paper instead summarizes noise by scalar SNR and entropy and proposes a Helmholtz free-energy description of whole stationary trajectories.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Thermodynamics: Entropic Forces in Deep and Universal Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural Thermodynamics develops entropic forces from stochasticity, finite steps, and symmetry breaking and connects them to representation alignment and both flatness- and sharpness-seeking. This paper gives a simpler scalar free-energy envelope for stationary LR sweeps and focuses on the UP-OP convergence split rather than learned representations.

competitive_landscape.title: Can Stationary Distributions of Scale-Invariant Neural Networks Be Described by the Thermodynamics of an Ideal Gas?
competitive_landscape.relationship: author follow-up and stronger thermodynamic formulation
competitive_landscape.difference: The follow-up derives temperature, pressure, volume, Gibbs-form stationary laws, and an ideal-gas equation for scale-invariant SGD with weight decay under explicit noise assumptions, then tests broader thermodynamic identities. It replaces much of this paper's post-hoc scalar fitting with a more structured theory but inherits equilibrium and entropy-estimation boundaries.

competitive_landscape.title: Does SGD Seek Flatness or Sharpness? An Exactly Solvable Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Xu et al. exactly solve a model in which SGD prefers minimum gradient fluctuations rather than flatness itself, with anisotropic label noise able to select arbitrarily sharp solutions, and reproduce the mechanism in MLPs, RNNs, and transformers. This directly cautions against reading scalar entropy maximization as a universal optimizer preference.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a self-consistent thermodynamic description in which fixed-LR SGD minimizes F=U-TS, with an empirically inferred temperature that rises with LR in stationary regimes and collapses toward zero for low-LR OP convergence; they further attribute the regime split to stochastic-gradient SNR near shared optima.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper supplies four architecture-dataset sweeps, a 28-point LR grid, k-NN trajectory-entropy estimates, fitted free-energy envelopes, low-LR time-local temperatures, gradient-norm subset sweeps, an exactly visualizable sphere example, and local SNR proofs. Primary records through 2026-08-24 show that free-energy, temperature, energy-entropy competition, finite-step noise, and noise-equilibrium mechanisms all predate the work, while later work from the same group substantially formalizes the analogy.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The narrow novelty is the empirical combination of post-hoc free-energy envelope fitting with an UP-versus-shared-zero-gradient OP comparison and the proposed SNR explanation. It is a useful organizing diagnostic, not evidence that SGD generally optimizes a unique physical free energy: the temperature is inferred from the same curve it fits, the entropy estimator is fragile, the tested models are specially projected, and the neural OP evidence falls short of the theory's ideal exponent. The 2026 ideal-gas follow-up is the stronger current formulation, while exact noise-selection work shows that scalar flatness or entropy preference is not universal.

reviewer_notes: Primary review and an independent secondary review covered every one of the 27 physical pages of arXiv:2505.23489v1, including all equations, the free-energy hypothesis box, Table 1, Figures 1-17 and their axes/captions, all references, the Helmholtz justification, full LR grids and smoothing rules, the SNR lemma and sphere theorem with their proofs, and all appendix ablations. The cached PDF and extracted-text SHA-256 values match fulltext_index.jsonl exactly, with usable text on all 27 pages. The arXiv record was checked on 2026-08-24 and remains v1. Eight direct primary competitor records were independently version-checked through that date. The official code repository was inspected at commit 912efa9263fc3e6ec1baf2665e53ec567305157e: it contains the training, entropy, SNR, toy, and plotting implementations but no raw experiment traces or locked environment; its README launch path passes --seed and --loss while run.py defines --seeds and --loss_fn, and requirements.txt omits the imported torchvision dependency. Quantitative statements preserve the paper's selected LR ranges and its approximately 0.78 gradient-decay exponent. Reviewer inferences remain labeled explicitly, especially the construction dependence of the free-energy minimum, uncertainty and estimator concerns, and the absence of predictive generalization tests.
